tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

The page doesn't include scoring criteria or Claude Code-specific setup steps, so I've left those out. Commands are reproduced exactly as shown. Other instructions are paraphrased.

**1. Install the CLI**

```
# macOS/Linux:
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash

# Windows:
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex
```

**2. Account signup and repo access**

- Sign in at entire.io with GitHub and authorize the Entire GitHub App when prompted. This can be done before or after importing the repo.
- A GitHub organization admin installs the Entire GitHub App on the organization through onboarding and imports the repository. Nothing appears for the team until this is done.
- Access follows the GitHub collaborator list. Changes can take up to an hour to sync. If the repo is missing, ask your org admin.

**3. Enable Entire in your repo and capture a session**

```
cd your-repo
entire enable
```

Start a new agent session, ask it for a focused change, and review the result.

**4. Commit and inspect the checkpoint**

```
git add path/to/changed-file
git commit -m "Build my first feature with Entire"
entire checkpoint list
entire checkpoint explain HEAD
```

When prompted, choose yes to link the commit to session context.

**5. Trails (feature-flagged)**

- Request access by filling in the Trails access form: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/REDACTED/viewform
- After Entire enables it, open your repo in Entire, go to **Settings → General**, and turn on **Runners**, **Auto build on push**, and **Trails**. This requires repository admin permission.
- From the repo root, run `entire runner setup -y`, then commit and push the generated `.entire/` files.
- Create a Trail by asking your agent or running `entire trail create`. Then commit and push to the Trail branch as usual.

**6. Continuous Memory (optional): entire-graph**

```
entire plugin install graph
entire graph init-agents --repo .
entire graph stats --repo .
```

Commit `.entire/graph-agent.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `CLAUDE.md`, then start a fresh agent session.

**7. Continuous Memory (optional): entire-brain**

Install from a prebuilt binary:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/entireio/entire-brain/main/scripts/get-brain.sh | bash
```

Or build from source (requires Go 1.27+, Git 2.36+, the Entire CLI on your PATH, and a C compiler):

```
git clone https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain.git
cd entire-brain
./scripts/install.sh
```

Then, in your project repo:

```
entire brain setup
entire brain init-agents
entire brain mcp --print-config
claude mcp add entire-brain -- entire brain mcp
```

Commit the generated agent instructions (`.entire/agent-guide.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`) when they should apply to your team.

**8. Troubleshooting and docs for your agent**

```
entire doctor
entire doctor --force
claude mcp add --transport http entire-docs https://docs.entire.io/mcp
```

`entire doctor --force` fixes issues without prompting. For non-MCP setups, point your agent to https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt.

**Agent integrations:** The page says Entire captures work from supported coding agents, and that you can add another through the Agent Integration Protocol. It doesn't give separate Claude Code setup steps. The agent integration guide is at https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/build-an-agent-integration

**Links**

- Quickstart: https://docs.entire.io/quickstart
- Checkpoints: https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/capture-checkpoints
- Graph setup: https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/set-up-graph
- Search: https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/search-in-cli
- Graph docs: https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/overview
- Doctor: https://docs.entire.io/cli-reference/doctor
- Entire sign-in: https://entire.io

- Brain agent guide: https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/blob/main/docs/reference.md#how-agents-use-the-brain
- Brain coordination contract: https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/blob/main/docs/agent-coordination.md

Here's the setup from the Entire hackathon guide. I checked your machine: the `entire` CLI isn't installed yet, `/Users/simon/hackathon` is empty and not a git repo yet, and `git` and `gh` are both installed.

## Required steps

**1. Install the CLI**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
```

**2. Sign in and connect GitHub**
- Go to https://entire.io, sign in with GitHub, and authorize the **Entire GitHub App** when asked.

**3. Enable Entire in your repo**

```bash
cd your-repo
entire enable
```
After that, start a **new** Claude Code session in the repo so Entire captures it.

**4. Commit and check that it's capturing**
```bash
git add <files>
git commit -m "..."        # answer "yes" when asked to link the commit to session context
entire checkpoint list
entire checkpoint explain HEAD
```
This is the part that gets scored. Each commit should link back to the agent session that produced it.

## Optional but worth it

**Trails** (Thomas's code-review demo)


**Pick "Mirror existing GitHub Repository"** (the right-hand card). The hackathon guide's whole flow assumes your code lives on GitHub:

- Repo access syncs from the GitHub collaborator list.
- Your teammates get in through the GitHub App.
- Trails, runners and auto build on push are all set up against a repo imported from GitHub.
- Judges and teammates will most likely look at your code on GitHub.

"Create new repository" hosts the code only on Entire. That's a newer, separate path the guide doesn't cover, and it adds risk you don't need this weekend.

**You need a GitHub repo before you can mirror it.** Your `hackathon` folder is empty and not a git repo yet, so do this first:

1. Create the GitHub repo. I can do it from here with `git init` and `gh repo create <name> --private --source . --push`. Just tell me the name and whether it should be private or under an org.
2. Go back to this screen, click **Mirror existing GitHub Repository**, install or authorize the Entire GitHub App, and pick the repo.
3. Locally, run the CLI install and `entire enable`, then start a fresh Claude Code session.

If a teammate already created the team repo on GitHub, skip step 1. Clone their repo and mirror that one instead, so you don't end up with two repos.

content.text:
**Go private for now, and make it public at submission if the rules ask for it.**

- **Private is safer while you build.** API keys and `.env` files tend to get committed in a hurry, and on a public repo bots scrape leaked keys within minutes. Private also keeps your idea away from other teams until you present.
- **Entire handles private repos fine.** Entire reads the repo through the GitHub App, and your teammates get access through the collaborator list, so visibility doesn't affect setup.
- **Switching later is easy.** On GitHub, go to Settings → General → Danger Zone → Change visibility. Mirroring isn't affected.

I couldn't check the submission rules: the Notion page loads its content with JavaScript, so my fetch came back empty. Look for a line about repo visibility or judges' code access in the submission section. If it says the repo must be public, flip it before the deadline. If judges only need access, adding them as collaborators works too.

If you're sure there are no secrets in the repo and the rules want open source, starting public is fine. It saves you one step at the end.

The message you pasted is from Entire, one of the sponsors. Its "How we score your submissions" line describes how Entire judges its own track, and the criterion is how well you used Entire to capture agent sessions. Without Entire set up, you have nothing to show them, so you'd score zero there.

I couldn't confirm whether the main judging requires sponsor tools, because the Notion page didn't load for me. Check its rules or judging section, or ask the organizers. Hackathons usually make sponsor tools optional and give each sponsor its own prize category.

My advice is to set it up anyway:

- **Setup is small:** install the CLI, mirror the repo, and run `entire enable`. It takes 10–15 minutes.
- **Day to day, it's free:** it records your Claude Code sessions in the background while you work as usual.
- **It's easy to win:** a sponsor track only gets scored against the teams that opted in.
- **It's hard to add later:** sessions you ran before setup aren't captured.

So decide now. If you're going for Entire's prize, set it up before you write real code.

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)

content.content:
Atira Challenges is a platform for agent hackathons in industrial sales. Teams build an agent system that works through business software using any model via the platform's proxy.

**Challenge:** *From RFQ to bid.* The agent reads a public tender, finds the current specification, checks prices and stock in the ERP, looks up the approved discount in the sales inbox, and submits one signed bid.

**Setup**
- **Install the CLI:** `curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh` (Windows: `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex`). The CLI needs Node 24, or the installer offers a private copy.
- **Log in:** a team member runs `atira login`. `atira token` prints your personal token.
- **Authentication:** send the token or run token in an `x-api-key` header or as `Authorization: Bearer`. Plain HTTP and curl work; the API guide covers the device flow.
- **Coding agent integration:** `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Claude Code) or `codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Codex). The MCP tools are `test_run`, `wait_for_run`, `diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_screenshot`, `run_inputs`, and `submit`.
- **Local testing:** `atira scout --env` runs your agent locally against the public websites.
- **Starter kit:** `starter-kit.tar.gz`, a minimal Python skeleton with `agent.json` at the root. It covers reading the run, connecting to browsers over CDP, and calling hosted models.

**Submission**
- Submit your agent as a gzipped tarball.
- Each submission runs once on the public dataset (public-1), which feeds the leaderboard.

**Final evaluation**
- Each team's latest submission that passed review runs once on a private dataset. Teams can opt in before the final run starts to have it run best of three.
- The private dataset uses different websites, content, and data, so don't overfit to the public scenario.

**Scoring and ranking**
- Leaderboard order: eligible answers first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time.
- Winners are chosen by private-dataset performance, then public-dataset performance, then system elegance.

**Rules**
- The model must decide at run time where to go, what to search for, and which documents matter.
- Fixed scripts or crawlers that collect the websites for one model call are rejected in review.
- Values copied from the websites into the code are rejected.

**Not covered in this page:** deadlines, environment variables, the scouting logins, and the answer format and quality metrics. The page points to the Getting started guide, the API guide, the scoring doc, and the OpenAPI description for these.

# Atira starter kit

A minimal starting point, not an agent. It does the platform plumbing: it reads the run, attaches to the run's
browsers and shows how to call the free hosted models. Then it stops at `solve()` in `agent.py`, the place for your
agent. Out of the box it exits without an answer.

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `run.py` | The run contract: reads the run (`load_run`) and submits an API answer (`submit_answer`) |
| `browsers.py` | Attaches to the run's browsers over CDP and gets a page (`connect`); locally it starts a Chromium |
| `models.py` | One call to each hosted model: `ask_qwen` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) and `ask_clef` (Cloudflare Clef) |
| `agent.py` | The entry point: reads the run, connects browser 1, calls `solve(task, page)` and submits what it returns |
| `agent.json` | How the sandbox installs (`uv sync`, the versions in `uv.lock`) and runs it; it waits for the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The plumbing against fakes |

## Your agent goes in `solve()`

`solve(task, page)` gets the run and a Playwright page in browser 1:

- `task["brief"]`: the task and its rules;
- `task["access"]`: each website's `siteId`, `url` and `credentials`;
- `task["submission"]`: where the answer goes, `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` or `{"kind": "site", "url": ...}`;
- `task["answer_schema"]`: the JSON Schema of the answer.

For an `api` submission, return the answer and `main()` submits it: `202` is accepted and final, `400` lists the
issues to fix. For a `site` submission, enter the answer on that website yourself and return `None`. Reading pages,
acting on them and working out the answer are yours to build.

Mind the clock: a scored run has 20 minutes, and `run.seconds_left(task)` says how many seconds are left. Every part
of the answer scores on its own, so submit your best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
searching; an answer that comes too late scores 0.

More browsers: set `"browsers": 2` (up to 4) in `agent.json`, then `await browsers.connect(playwright, 1)` attaches
to browser 2.

## The hosted models in short

Both are free and need no key of yours: runs get the variables, and locally `atira scout --env` sets them, pointed
at `atira models proxy`.

```python
import models

text = await models.ask_qwen("Which button submits this form? ...")          # QWEN_BASE_URL, QWEN_API_KEY
yes = await models.ask_clef({"page": page_text}, "Is this the current revision?")  # CLEF_BASE_URL, CLEF_API_KEY
```

`models.qwen()` is an OpenAI SDK client, for tool calls, images and everything else. Clef is set only where the
platform hosts it; if your agent relies on it, list `"models": ["qwen", "clef"]` in `agent.json` so the run waits for
it to warm up. Another provider works with your own key through the run's metering proxy:
`$API/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls`.

## Run it locally

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) (open a new terminal after installing it, so
it is on your PATH) and the Atira CLI, signed in once with `atira login`.

Terminal 1: start the free models and leave it open.

```sh
atira models proxy
```

Terminal 2, in this folder:

```sh
uv sync && uv run playwright install chromium
```

A minimal starting point, not an agent. It does the platform plumbing: it reads the run, attaches to the run's

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `run.py` | The run contract: reads the run (`load_run`) and submits an API answer (`submit_answer`) |
| `browsers.py` | Attaches to the run's browsers over CDP and gets a page (`connect`); locally it starts a Chromium |
| `models.py` | One call to each hosted model: `ask_qwen` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) and `ask_clef` (Cloudflare Clef) |
| `agent.py` | The entry point: reads the run, connects browser 1, calls `solve(task, page)` and submits what it returns |
| `agent.json` | How the sandbox installs (`uv sync`, the versions in `uv.lock`) and runs it; it waits for the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The plumbing against fakes |

## Your agent goes in `solve()`

`solve(task, page)` gets the run and a Playwright page in browser 1:

- `task["brief"]`: the task and its rules;
- `task["access"]`: each website's `siteId`, `url` and `credentials`;
- `task["submission"]`: where the answer goes, `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` or `{"kind": "site", "url": ...}`;
- `task["answer_schema"]`: the JSON Schema of the answer.

For an `api` submission, return the answer and `main()` submits it: `202` is accepted and final, `400` lists the
issues to fix. For a `site` submission, enter the answer on that website yourself and return `None`. Reading pages,
acting on them and working out the answer are yours to build.

Mind the clock: a scored run has 20 minutes, and `run.seconds_left(task)` says how many seconds are left. Every part
of the answer scores on its own, so submit your best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
searching; an answer that comes too late scores 0.

content.content:
# Atira Challenges

> Atira Challenges is a platform for agent hackathons in industrial sales. Teams build an agent system (one agent or several) that works through realistic business software, with any model through our proxy and their own tools. Each scored submission is reviewed automatically, run in an isolated sandbox on the public dataset, and ranked on a live leaderboard: eligible answers first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time. When the hackathon ends, every team's latest submission that passed review runs once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

The public pages are also Markdown: the home page, Getting started, each challenge, its leaderboard and each team's profile. Add `.md` to the URL (`/index.md` for the home page) or send `Accept: text/markdown`. For runs, use the API or the CLI's MCP tools. Everything works with plain HTTP, so `curl` and the API guide are enough. Send your personal token (`atira token` prints it after `atira login`; plain curl can use the device flow in the API guide) or the run token in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

If you are a team's coding agent: install the CLI (`curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh`, on Windows `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex`), have a team member run `atira login`, then add the CLI as your MCP server: `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Claude Code) or `codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Codex). Its tools start test runs (`test_run`), wait for them (`wait_for_run`), show why one failed (`diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_screenshot`, `run_inputs`) and submit (`submit`); [Debug runs from your coding agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md) lists them all. Run the agent locally against the public websites with `atira scout --env`, and start from the starter kit below. The agent you build must let a model choose where to go, what to search for and which documents matter, at run time: fixed scripts and crawlers that collect the websites for one model call are rejected in review, and so are values copied from the websites into the code.

Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too. When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

The [leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) shows the public dataset until the organizers publish the final results.

## Start here

- [Getting started](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start.md): what you're building, your first run step by step with every command, the scouting logins for the websites, the rules of the game and how you're scored
- [The starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz): a minimal Python skeleton to start from (reading the run, the browsers over CDP, the hosted models; the agent is yours to build), as a gzipped tarball with `agent.json` at its root

## Challenges

- [From RFQ to bid](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md): Your agent reads a public tender, finds the current specification, checks prices and stock in the ERP, looks up the approved discount in the sales inbox and submits one signed bid.
- [From RFQ to bid: leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md): the ranked results of scored submissions
- [From RFQ to bid: public dataset board](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md?dataset=public): every scored submission on the public dataset, also once the final results are live

## Taking part

- [Participant guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/README.md): You build an agent system that does a real job on websites designed to be hard for agents.
- [Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md): Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and ranks everyone the same way.
- [How a run works](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md): A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge.
- [Building your agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/building-an-agent.md): Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes the decisions, at run time.
- [Fair play](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md): You submit an agentic system: one agent or several.
- [Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md): You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball.
- [Demo day](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/demo-day.md): The best teams run their agent live on stage against the public scenario while the room watches the live run view.
- [FAQ and event details](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/faq.md)

## API

- [OpenAPI 3.1 description](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/openapi.json): every participant endpoint, with credentials, request bodies (including the gzip upload), responses and errors
- [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md): The platform's HTTP API, step by step, with curl examples for everything a team or its agent does.

## Optional

## Quick start for agents

Set the platform URL, install the CLI and sign in once: `atira login` opens the browser, where you approve a personal token for this device (`atira login --device` prints a link and a code instead, for a machine without a browser; plain curl uses the [device flow](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in)). Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

```sh
export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh   # the CLI for Node 24; read it first: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less

eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites, to run your agent locally
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq   # one sandbox run on the public dataset, opened live
atira submit ./my-agent --challenge rfq     # review, then the scored run on the public dataset
atira status
```

## The task

One tender, four German websites, one bid.

The agent produces: **One bid**. It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.

## The websites

Each run gets its own logins, in the run's `access`. To look around yourself, use the scouting logins below. Expect what real business software throws at you: popups, session timeouts, outdated documents and look-alike records. Everything your agent needs fits on a 1280×800 screen.

### 1. Tender portal (Vergabeportal, `tender-portal`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-tender-portal.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: The public tender, its bill of quantities, the bidder Q&A that changes quantities, and the bid configurator.
- What makes it hard: Cookie wall, flaky error pages, documents behind an expression of interest, iframes and ZIP files, a deadline in another timezone.

### 2. Supplier portal (Lieferantenportal, `customer-portal`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-customer-portal.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: The buyer's technical specification and its revisions.
- What makes it hard: Opens the oldest revision first, nested document viewers, paged requirement tables.

### 3. ERP (`erp`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-erp.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your company's materials, stock, lead times and price conditions with validity periods and quantity scales.
- What makes it hard: SAP-style transaction codes, an F4 search popup, status codes, a short session timeout.

### 4. Webmail (Werkpost, `mail`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-mail.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your sales inbox, with the sales director's discount approval and the signing TAN.
- What makes it hard: Look-alike approvals for other tenders, superseded approvals, an archive folder, paging.

## Public and private data

There are two datasets. The leaderboard uses the public one, on these websites. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.

- **Public dataset:** The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too.
- **Private dataset (the final run):** When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

## Bid rules

The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.

1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.

## How a run works

Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).

1. **Start.** The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
2. **Read.** Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
3. **Work the websites.** It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
5. **Scored.** The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.

### Develop locally

```sh
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting"   # the same, with the brief, as JSON
# run your agent on your machine, then once in the sandbox:
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq
```

`atira scout --env` exports the scouting logins as `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the shape a run gets), each website's URL, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the brief and the answer format. It also points the free hosted models at `atira models proxy` on your computer, so your agent needs no model key; another provider takes your own. Nothing done there counts. With these logins, an answer entered on the tender portal is acknowledged but never counts. In a run, your agent reads the same at `GET /v1/runs/current` with the run token as `x-api-key`, and hands in one valid answer of up to 65,536 bytes; a malformed one returns its problems while the clock keeps running.

### Read the run

Inside a test or scored run, with the run token (`$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`) in `RUN_TOKEN`:

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/runs/current" -H "x-api-key: $RUN_TOKEN"
```

The response holds `brief` (the task in Markdown, with the rules), `access` (each website's `url` and `credentials`), `submission` (where the answer goes), `answer_schema`, `expires_at`, `llm_proxy_url` and `llm_providers`. Outside a run, `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` returns the brief, logins, answer target and schema for the public websites, without a token.

We host Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare's Clef for this hackathon, free and with no usage cap. #6 on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-8-flash-next) (open-weight, large models). Multimodal general-purpose LLM. ### Cloudflare Clef

A multimodal decision model. Give it a state and up to 4 screenshots, then ask it questions: `choice` picks one of your options, `noul` gives the probability of yes, from 0 to 1, and `score` rates on a scale you set. See [Cloudflare's announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clef-decision-models/) and [the benchmarks](https://clef-evals.workers-ai-mle.workers.dev). Worth a try for quick, low-stakes decisions, such as which link to open or whether a page is the right document, while the bigger model reads and reasons.

- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 16 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
- **Simulated pricing:**

  - Output: Not priced

```sh
    "criteria": {

      "report": "Report the error"}}}}'
```

In a run, `QWEN_BASE_URL` with `QWEN_API_KEY` and `CLEF_BASE_URL` with `CLEF_API_KEY` are set for you. An idle model can take several minutes to wake on its first call, so use long timeouts.

```sh

atira models proxy   # keep it running; it prints:

export QWEN_API_KEY=local
```

## Submitting

A submission is your agent as a gzipped tarball. It is reviewed automatically, then run once in the sandbox on the public dataset, and that score ranks your team. Submit as often as you like, one at a time; your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.

### agent.json

```json
{
  "setup": ["uv", "sync"],
  "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"],
  "models": ["qwen"]
}
```

Put `agent.json` at the root of the tarball, next to your code and its dependency file. Up to 20 MB compressed. `setup` installs dependencies with network access, within 5 minutes that don't count toward your time; `run` is timed and reaches only the platform and the websites. `"browsers": 1–4` (default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts, each on its own screen. `"models"` lists the hosted models your agent calls; the run waits only for those to warm up (for all of them when it's absent). Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, and Rust with cargo are installed. The [starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal skeleton to start from.

```sh
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
  "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions"
```

Or drop the tarball on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). Upload it as a test run first to watch it work in the sandbox: its browser live, its logs, and a recording afterwards.

## Scoring and ranking

Every submission is measured on its run in the sandbox.

- **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
- **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
- **Cost:** Every model call goes through the proxy and is priced per model. There is no budget: at equal quality, cost × time decides.
- **Time:** Wall-clock time from the start of the run until the answer is accepted. It weighs as much as cost: halving either halves cost × time.

Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.

Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.

## Leaderboard

**Public dataset.** Eligible first, then quality, then cost × time. The top ten; the [full leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) has every team.

No team has a scored submission yet. Test runs don't appear here.

Your agent has to find the answer itself.

- Your system must work the answer out from the websites at run time, with a model doing the navigating and deciding. A coding agent reviews every package; hardcoded answers, fixed scripts and crawlers are rejected.
- Bring your own model key for Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Together, Fireworks, kept as a team secret. Every call goes through the run's proxy and is metered at the published prices. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef are ours, unlimited. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair. The sandbox reaches the platform and the websites, nothing else.
- At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up to 4 in agent.json ("browsers"), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The sandbox stops any other browser your agent starts.
- One submission in flight per team. Submit again once it has finished.

## Public and private data

There are two datasets. The leaderboard uses the public one, on these websites. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.

- **Public dataset:** The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too.
- **Private dataset (the final run):** When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.

1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.

## How a run works

Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).

1. **Start.** The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
2. **Read.** Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
3. **Work the websites.** It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
5. **Scored.** The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.

### Develop locally

```sh
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting"   # the same, with the brief, as JSON
# run your agent on your machine, then once in the sandbox:
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq
```

`atira scout --env` exports the scouting logins as `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the shape a run gets), each website's URL, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the brief and the answer format. It also points the free hosted models at `atira models proxy` on your computer, so your agent needs no model key; another provider takes your own. Nothing done there counts. With these logins, an answer entered on the tender portal is acknowledged but never counts. In a run, your agent reads the same at `GET /v1/runs/current` with the run token as `x-api-key`, and hands in one valid answer of up to 65,536 bytes; a malformed one returns its problems while the clock keeps running.

### Read the run

Inside a test or scored run, with the run token (`$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`) in `RUN_TOKEN`:

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/runs/current" -H "x-api-key: $RUN_TOKEN"
```

The response holds `brief` (the task in Markdown, with the rules), `access` (each website's `url` and `credentials`), `submission` (where the answer goes), `answer_schema`, `expires_at`, `llm_proxy_url` and `llm_providers`. Outside a run, `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` returns the brief, logins, answer target and schema for the public websites, without a token.

## Unlimited Inference

We host Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare's Clef for this hackathon, free and with no usage cap. On your laptop, `atira models proxy` gives you a URL and key (setup on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team#team-models)). In test and scored runs it's set up for you. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair.

### Qwen3.8-Flash-Next

#6 on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-8-flash-next) (open-weight, large models). Multimodal general-purpose LLM. Strong at reasoning, tool calls and reading pages and screenshots, with a 256k context, so it can plan, browse and write the answer.

- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 32 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
- **Simulated pricing:**
  - Input: $0.15 / M tokens
  - Cached input: $0.016 / M tokens
  - Cache writes: Free
  - Output: $0.47 / M tokens
- **Precision:** [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4) (NVIDIA's checkpoint)

Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

qwen = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.environ["QWEN_BASE_URL"],
    api_key=os.environ["QWEN_API_KEY"],
)
reply = qwen.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen",
    messages=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Which button submits?",
    }],
)
```

### Cloudflare Clef

A multimodal decision model. Give it a state and up to 4 screenshots, then ask it questions: `choice` picks one of your options, `noul` gives the probability of yes, from 0 to 1, and `score` rates on a scale you set. See [Cloudflare's announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clef-decision-models/) and [the benchmarks](https://clef-evals.workers-ai-mle.workers.dev). Worth a try for quick, low-stakes decisions, such as which link to open or whether a page is the right document, while the bigger model reads and reasons.

- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 16 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
- **Simulated pricing:**
  - Input: $0.24 / M tokens
  - Output: Not priced

Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.

```sh
curl "$CLEF_BASE_URL/v1/decide" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLEF_API_KEY" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "state": {"page": "Checkout returns 502"},
  "questions": {"next": {
    "type": "choice",
    "instructions": "What next?",
    "criteria": {
      "retry": "Retry the request",
      "report": "Report the error"}}}}'
```

In a run, `QWEN_BASE_URL` with `QWEN_API_KEY` and `CLEF_BASE_URL` with `CLEF_API_KEY` are set for you. On your machine, `atira models proxy` serves the same APIs on 127.0.0.1, so the same code works in both. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. An idle model can take several minutes to wake on its first call, so use long timeouts.

```sh
atira login   # once per computer
atira models proxy   # keep it running; it prints:
export QWEN_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/qwen/v1
export QWEN_API_KEY=local
export CLEF_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/clef
export CLEF_API_KEY=local
```

Cost and time count toward your rank, and a call to these models costs a fraction of a frontier call. Use them for the easy steps.

If one fails mid-run, retry the call, as with any provider. If they were down for most of a run that then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count, and a scored run starts again once by itself.

## Submitting

A submission is your agent as a gzipped tarball. It is reviewed automatically, then run once in the sandbox on the public dataset, and that score ranks your team. Submit as often as you like, one at a time; your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.

### agent.json

```json
{
  "setup": ["uv", "sync"],
  "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"],
  "models": ["qwen"]
}
```

Put `agent.json` at the root of the tarball, next to your code and its dependency file. Up to 20 MB compressed. `setup` installs dependencies with network access, within 5 minutes that don't count toward your time; `run` is timed and reaches only the platform and the websites. `"browsers": 1–4` (default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts, each on its own screen. `"models"` lists the hosted models your agent calls; the run waits only for those to warm up (for all of them when it's absent). Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, and Rust with cargo are installed. The [starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal skeleton to start from.

### Upload

```sh
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
  "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions"
```

Or drop the tarball on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). Upload it as a test run first to watch it work in the sandbox: its browser live, its logs, and a recording afterwards.

## Scoring and ranking

Every submission is measured on its run in the sandbox.

- **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
- **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
- **Cost:** Every model call goes through the proxy and is priced per model. There is no budget: at equal quality, cost × time decides.
- **Time:** Wall-clock time from the start of the run until the answer is accepted. It weighs as much as cost: halving either halves cost × time.

Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.

Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.

## Leaderboard

**Public dataset.** Eligible first, then quality, then cost × time. The top ten; the [full leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) has every team.
